title: Mark Zuckerberg on AI's Job Impact, Government Regulation, & How Meta Glasses Changed His Routine
summary: Zuckerberg 做客 Idea Generation 现场特辑，谈 AI 对就业的冲击、政府监管、Meta 眼镜如何改变他的日常，以及 Meta 的 AI 路线。
title_zh: Mark Zuckerberg 谈 AI 对就业的冲击、政府监管，与 Meta 眼镜如何改变他的日常

transcripts.content: What is the best way to ensure that we have a positive future if the technology development continues on its trajectory? >> In 2004, a young man in Harvard University's Kirkland House had an idea. Obsessed with the intersection of personal computing and social networking, Mark Zuckerberg pushed his personal programming project, then known as The Facebook, live. And in that small act, revolutionized social media and changed global culture forever. In the years that followed, Zuckerberg would scale Facebook's audience and influence [music] beyond his or anyone's wildest imagination. He would then leverage that success into a consolidation of power, rolling up a litany of other platforms, including Instagram, WhatsApp, and Oculus, eventually renaming the parent company Meta. Throughout this meteoric rise, Zuckerberg and Meta would live up to the company's founding ethos, moving fast and breaking things. However, the wins would always outpace the missteps, and 22 years later, the once upstart iconoclast [music] is now a global institution. On June 23rd, 2026, in New York City, we sat down with Zuckerberg for a special live taping of Idea Generation to discuss all of this, as well as the launch of his latest market leader, Meta's AI glasses. And it all started with one idea. >> [applause] [music] >> Hello. Welcome, everyone. Thank you for joining us for this live taping of Idea Generation. I think it goes without saying that there is not a creative entrepreneur on the planet who has been more responsible for crafting the reality that we all share than the gentleman that sits next to me, Mark Zuckerberg. >> [applause] >> Thank you for joining us. >> Yeah, well, this is this is a big day for us, so thank you for doing this. This is great timing. You know, we're super We are we're very excited for um for the announcements today. The um you know, the the new line of Meta glasses, it's uh it's the first line of glasses that we've designed with our partner EssilorLuxottica from the ground up. Um you know, so this builds on the work that we've been doing with Ray-Ban and Oakley and iconic brands and it basically brings all of that functionality to um a a new line that um we hope will be accessible to a lot more people, but brings all of the functionality including the most advanced AI models that we've built right into the the glasses. So, we're we're we're very happy to to to be doing this. >> What is it about the form factor of glasses that draws you to you know, to think that that will be sort of the next I guess version of the phone maybe? >> Yeah, so I guess there's a few things overall that make us optimistic that glasses are the next computing platform. One is that you've you kind of have this trajectory over time where computing gets to be more natural and more integrated in our lives and glasses just give you the opportunity to interact with technology but remain present with the people around you, which I think is a really fundamentally important thing that obviously phones don't do. When you interact with your phone, you're kind of interacting with this you know, small rectangle. It pulls you away from the world around you. You want to um have technology be able to um effectively fully integrate with the world around you. So, that's a big one. Another piece is that glasses are the ideal form factor for you to be able to give an AI assistant uh that that works for you the ability to see what you see, hear what you hear, talk to you throughout the day and then eventually also can display information in your field of view and and be able to overlay things on the world around you. So, that's something that you can get parts of that with other form factors. You might be able to you know, if you have earbuds, maybe it can hear what you hear, and maybe it can it can talk to you. But, I think the visual part is going to be very important. And obviously, glasses I think are the ideal form factor for that. And then one one more thing is just is just that glasses are very It's It's a thing that people have, right? I mean, it's there's you know, almost 2 billion people in the world wear optical glasses already. And billions more wear sunglasses. So, I kind of think we're at this moment now where it's kind of like, you know, everyone had smart had had had normal Everyone had flip phones, and then you got smartphones came out. And it just kind of became It felt pretty clear that in 5 years or whatever, all of the flip phones were going to be smartphones. And that's basically, you know, how I feel about glasses today. It's like, what is the reason why 5 years from now any of the glasses that people wear are not going to be able to have this kind of functionality to help people out throughout their day. It just doesn't quite make sense. So, I think it's a very natural um design that people are used to. >> How long ago did you have this revelation? And sort of, you know, once you seize upon this idea, what are the dominoes that you have to start setting up? >> Well, I mean, we've been working on this I think since 2014. Right? I think the the earliest um part of our work on, you know, we started working on virtual reality and augmented reality. And the the notion is that, okay, virtual reality, you know, allows you to do some of the augmentation of the world in a somewhat larger form factor before you get into the one that people are going to wear every day. But, some of the glasses that we've been working on it's more than 10 years at this point. I think that the partnership with with Essilor Luxottica, you know, we've done multiple generations starting with the the original Ray-Bans that we did. And then it just each year we've added more functionality. It's gotten to uh you know, it adds more functionalities to So, now, you know, you can do phone calls, you can like listen to music. It has all this um functionality to help people who might not be able to see. If If someone can't uh can't hear well, it can it can amplify the the hearing in their ears. Like, all the all the different functionality you just kind of add generation over generation. The AI keeps on getting better. Now, I think we're I mean, we're going to be working on this for for decades more, but I think this is like the This is I think the next 5 years are going to be a really key period for this. >> You have had access to these probably longer than almost anyone on the planet. How have they changed your daily routine? >> The The main thing that I notice is just There are a lot of things that you could do on your phone. But if you have glasses on, it's just better. All right, so it being able to talk to like take phone calls and have your ear open and not occluded. So, it's like, all right, I'm just walking down the street and you can like hear what's going on. I think that's really nice. Um the fact that the microphone is in the nose pad, so the clarity of the audio that it picks up is so high that you could literally be in a wind tunnel and it would sound completely clear to the person on the other side. I mean, I've taken business calls on like a jet ski. >> Not often, but um >> it has happened. And the other person could not tell that I was on it It's great, right? It's like, that's good. You don't necessarily want to tell the other person that you're on a jet ski. So, I I think that that that kind of stuff is is nice, but the the main way that I think that this is going to work is that you know, it's not like all the other computing platforms go away, right? When we started using phones, our computers didn't go away. We still have computers, but I don't know how many of you feel this way, but I'm often I'm sitting at my desk, my computer is right there, but I still just reach for my phone to go send someone a message or something, right? Cuz it's just the phone has kind of become the primary platform. And I think similarly, glasses are going to be that. So, I think as you can do more and more with the glasses, we'll just kind of be in a world where you're you'll have your phone with you, but it'll just kind of stay in the pocket more of the time. And then maybe eventually you'll leave it at home more of the time. But I don't I don't think that, you know, in the next 10 years we're going to stop having phones or something like that. I just think that glasses are going to each generation become more and more the primary thing that we use and and you know, just be more integrated into our lives. >> Having started this in 2014, I know that Meta is very early or it has been very early on the AI wave and you know, responsible for a lot of like early machine learning in the 2010s, long before anyone in this crowd was interacting with an LLM. There have been revolutionary steps that have taken place in the last 6 months, 12 months. >> Totally. >> How has that changed sort of how you think about what is inside the glasses and how people will use them? >> So, one of the neat things is that if you get the hardware package right, hardware is kind of slow, right? So, we we've been planning like this generation of glasses for whatever, 2 years whatever the the the cycle is for that and you know, we're planning the you know, 2028 line of glasses now, right? And and all that. Then you get all these releases in between that are basically just the AI getting better and better. So, if you buy these glasses today, they're just going to keep on getting more and more useful for you as the AI becomes more powerful and able to do more things. So, the biggest advances in the last couple of years I I'd say there's the the simple one on multimodal understanding, right? So, just being able to not just ask it a question, but actually have it be able to see what's going on around you and be able to to to kind of talk to you about that is is quite helpful. And obviously language translation at this point is almost solved, right? So, you have the real-time translation built into it. So, you travel to another place, it can it can basically speak to you and it and then and translate another language. But one of the things that I'm really excited about is the advance in the agentic AI. So, what I guess I I mean by that is moving away from this use pattern where you ask it a question and it's one question, one answer, right? It's what what I think this is going to evolve more towards is either you give it a task and it goes away and thinks and then comes back a a bit later or you [snorts] just have these like live sessions where you know, it's like I'm cooking, I'm like baking something with my daughter and I'm terrible at this, and I'm just trying to do it to hang out with my 3-year-old who's into baking, and like it can basically just it's like no, really don't do that. Like do this instead. And it's like, okay, that's good. I didn't even have to ask it. It just it's watching, right? It knows. Um Like do not do not put the flour there. Um so, that I think is um that is is really good. Right? And and basically as you tune the the exam as you tune the system, you can go from you know, half an hour of of like the always-on AI to an hour to 2 hours to eventually that's like just all day. Right? And then that's a very different mode of using the AI where now if obviously you'll have control over how it's how your um when when you want it to be on and not, but you can see that like pretty quickly I think we're going to get to the zone where you you effectively have the ability for your AI to see what you see, hear what you hear, summarize that, help you out with all of these things throughout the day, and it just kind of amazing when you plug this stuff into an AI, how much of the signal that we have throughout our day that we just kind of miss or we, you know, we tune stuff out cuz we're focused on something, but there's something else happening that was important, or someone said something in a conversation, and you know, so it's kind of the ability to have that kind of memory or be able to help you in all these ways is going to be incredibly important. >> How do you sort of normalize cuz there are this does allow you to be present, but it is somewhat intrusive in your life and particularly if it is helping you and actively engaging in everything that you >> you want to make sure I think so, our mantra for designing the glasses is that they have to be great glasses first. I guess what we mean is that the technology is secondary, the fashion and the wearing it is actually primary, which is kind of it was an interesting thing for us to get there as a technology company because I think and and I think all of most of the technology companies think about it is like, all right, we're trying to cram all this technology into it. It's like this shape looks kind of like the glasses that they put out. Like why wouldn't why won't why won't people wear this? But it's I I think it's like like I think the reality is that you're going to wear the glasses you like whatever glasses you have you're going to wear for many hours and you're going to use the technology for some small fraction of it. And it's actually really important. So in order to unlock that, it needs to be that the glasses are something that you're proud to wear and they need to be comfortable so that way you'll wear them for for long periods of time. So they have to be great glasses first. Part of that also means getting out of the way. Right? So I think a lot of technology companies kind of have the vision of oh well we can help you here and we can help you here and we can help you here and like okay let's just kind of like bombard you with stuff and it's like people don't want that. I don't want that. Right? It's like I I think you actually want it to be very sparing in terms of when it will ping you or interrupt you on something. So that's kind of the way that we think about it is great glasses first, technology available when you want it with more and more capabilities, but we really don't want it to be intrusive. >> I was watching an interview that you gave I guess the last fall around the release of the latest Ray-Bans. And you were just sort of talking about your vision for AI in general and how you were trying to articulate I guess the idea that there would be sort of bespoke models then that people would sort of curate their own sort of suite of AI that they use. And I'm I'm curious a year later cuz there has been quite a bit of innovation in the field. Is that still how you see it all playing out? >> Yeah. So our vision for what we're trying to build on the AI side we call personal super intelligence. And the the idea I I think it's very different from what the kind of consensus view of all of the other AI labs is. I think most other companies that are working on AI think that there's going to be like you know one big AI that everyone uses or that it's kind of like doing stuff for the world and I don't know. I mean maybe this is just a legacy that we have of and we you know from the history of the company building social media. It's all about building tools, putting them in people's hands, believing that people should have agency to use the tools and express the things that they want to. Um in that there's fundamentally this view I don't know, I think that in order to have a good future with a strong AI, you want a lot of like checks and balances. All right, so I don't I I I don't want to live in a future where there's like one big AI. I think that's a bad future. No matter how good the AI is, I think like that's not good. I think the way that this ends up being good is you actually just you you direct um the technology development towards empowering every individual. And the reality is that individuals, people have different aspirations. And the aspirations sometimes overlap with each other and sometimes they compete with each other. And that competition is important because it's that is sort of the our society and markets' way of putting checks and balances on the way that things work. And I think in a world where kind of everyone has a personal superintelligence that has the context that you want it to have because you have whatever devices you you you have that can can give it the context that you want it to have about your life. And it can help you achieve your goals and work on your behalf 24/7. And as many people around the world as possible have that, to me that's the best shot that we have of getting to a future that is like really good. Right? It's like that in that world I think people are empowered, but also you you kind of have a fundamental kind of check on on this and there's a balance of of power and how that works. So I think that that I think is just a very fundamental thing for our philosophy. And everything that we're developing from the kind of AI software and the models and the technology to the idea of the the hardware and that the glasses and different things that we'll make to make it so people can use this in different ways. It's kind of all in the service of of that of that philosophy. >> You mentioned the sort of checks and balances and the importance of that. I I don't know if you're familiar with the book that came out last fall, if anyone builds it, everyone dies. I'm I'm a bit curious. Do you think that there's any credence to that kind of uh you know doomer concern around the implications of AI. >> I guess I'm not as familiar with that book, but I mean but I think the the the concept of of kind of AI safety is obviously a very important one, right? So, I guess I'm a little more optimistic than that. I don't think if anyone builds it everyone will die, but I I do think that there are anything that is a powerful new technology gives people the ability to do good things and it can give people the ability to do bad things. And the more powerful the lever that you're giving people, the more good and the more harm that they can potentially do. So, obviously taking that very seriously and working to mitigate the harm while making it as positive as possible for people is incredibly important. But that's where you get to this philosophy that I was talking about which is what is the best way to ensure that we have a positive future if the technology development continues on its trajectory? I think some people would say, "Okay, what you want to do is build a singular AI and make it like as aligned as possible." And I I just I I don't know that that's going to be enough, right? I think like because I I think the reality is this, if you have one thing that is super powerful, I don't know. I mean there have been a lot of like you know, people or or you know, regimes that get absolute power over time and that usually just doesn't end well, right? No matter how enlightened the the thing is. And I think humans are limited in our ability to build enlightenment into a thing no matter how hard we try. So, I kind of think that there is a natural mechanism that humanity and civilization has which are checks and balances. So, my version of this is in terms of creating a positive future is not that you have one central thing, but I think it's like you really need it to be widely distributed. And it's in some ways it's it's somewhat of a controversial concept because I think some people would say, "Oh, well if you like if you if you give a very like a model or an AI that has a lot of capabilities to individuals, won't they do bad things?" But I don't know. I think that this is always been a historical tension between liberty and empowering individuals and um in how you build society. And I think at every step along the way we tend to, you know, benefit when we try to like go for, you know, giving people more freedom and more agency and not saying, "Oh, this is This is too much for a person to handle." We want people to have the the individual agency to do that. Now, I think that that's the path to to a better future. So, I think we do that. I'm I'm I'm I'm pretty optimistic about the future. But, I don't know. >> The different people are trying to are trying to build different things. So, I hope our vision is the one that gets built. >> I'm curious cuz, you know, you were obviously instrumental in the creation of social media as we know it and obviously dealt with second and third-order consequences. Some surprising and positive, some that had to be mitigated. With AI, what are the things on the horizon that you think people are not expecting that will sort of enliven society or, you know, present potential dangers? >> Yeah, so I guess the ones that most people are focused on right now is you're having this huge ability for the AI to be able to code, which is helpful because even for people who are not engineers, um there's just a lot of coding that you want it to be able to do. So, it's like I don't know, I I put um I have this agent, I like put cameras up in in my MMA gym and I'm like, "All right, can you just watch me and like give me feedback in between rounds?" And it's like, "All right, that's actually a coding problem." Right? Cuz now it has to like deal with the the the kind of video pipeline of of processing all the the image frames that come in and piping that in and figuring out when like I'm in between rounds and then sending me the thing. So, obviously the better that stuff gets at coding, the better it gets at being able to, you know, you get more cybersecurity threats. I think that that's obviously one of the big topics now. I I think one of the things on the horizon that I think we're going to start seeing more scientific advances. So, my like philanthropic work outside of Meta, Priscilla and I created this thing BioHub where our our goal is to help advance the pace of scientific research in order to help scientists cure and prevent disease like all diseases this century. And when we started that we thought that that was like really ambitious. Okay, like cure and prevent all diseases this century. Now it's probably too conservative. Like I think it it like I don't know if it's going to be a decade or two decades or whatever, but I I would guess it'll be much sooner than the end of the century when when when you get there. And I think a lot of that is because of the progress of building these AI models that can effectively simulate biology and therefore help with drug design and help with understanding of fundamental parts of biology and how to get the right equilibrium for how all that works. But, you know, the things that can create that, I think there's the concern that well, could someone who's bad use that to make things that hurt people, right? Or create like a bio weapon or something. And I think that that's still an open question, but I think it's clearly a thing that really needs to be thought through carefully. And and I think it's one of the things on the on the horizon that we need to be careful about. So, I think that those are probably the two in the next year or two that I think there's a path to unlock a huge amount of value and also I think a clear roadmap to mitigate some of the concerns, but also pretty big concerns that that I think you want to be careful about. And then, you know, once you get beyond that, I think you start getting into these broader societal questions around like the balance of power and stuff that we talked about a minute ago that I think are just going to be really fundamental. You know, people talk about stuff like you know, obviously there's a lot of anxiety about job displacement. Companies are always trying to do things more efficiently, right? It's like I'm I'm sure you you do, right? If you if you have a task, you don't want to just keep on doing the same task. You try to find a way to, you know, do it more efficiently. And at the same time, people are people kind of improve their own productivity. Well, there's a natural balance of this stuff, right? So, if companies get very good at automating stuff faster than individuals get better at productivity, then you'd kind of assume that the number of jobs might decrease, but I think that people assume that that's an inevitability. I don't actually think it is. I think if you focus on empowering people and making people more productive, and that happens at a faster rate than companies get better at automating things, then in theory there should be more jobs in the future, not less. So, I think that's why like you need this balance, right? If like if you just have a few companies and they're focused on automating all knowledge work, then like all right, I don't know. That's probably not a great future, right? But if you if you have like a balance where some companies are focused on making it so that companies can work more efficiently, but others are, you know, focused on more of this personal superintelligence vision where you're like empowering individuals and making people more productive at each step along the way, then like I think it's probably going to be pretty good. So, I don't know. I think that this is just all stuff that you want to think through and be careful about, but um but I think that there is a path forward that can be very positive on this. >> Well, you mentioned the cyber cybersecurity thing, which obviously everyone's talking about with um Anthropic having to roll back Mythos.
